source_metadata.title: Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction

extraction_metadata.secondary_source_guardrail: Trial and guideline findings are represented as the review authors reports, tagged secondary_reported_result where applicable, and are not represented as if this publication enrolled those trial participants.

atoms.canonical_statement: The Clinical Practice article reviews the evaluation and treatment of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction using a case vignette, evidence summaries, formal guidelines, and the authors clinical recommendations.

The Journal feature states that it begins with a case vignette, presents evidence supporting management strategies, reviews formal guidelines when available, and ends with the authors clinical recommendations.

The article defines heart failure with preserved ejection fraction as heart failure with left ventricular ejection fraction of at least 50 percent, heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction as 41 to 49 percent, and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction as 40 percent or less.
The review states that heart failure with preserved ejection fraction accounts for up to 50 percent of adults hospitalized with heart failure.
The review reports that HFpEF prevalence increased from 38 percent in the late 1980s to 54 percent in the early 2000s.
The review reports an adult HFpEF incidence of 7 to 18 cases per 1000 persons per year.

The review describes HFpEF as a heterogeneous syndrome associated with aging and cardiometabolic disease and notes frequent obesity, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease, and noncardiovascular comorbidity.
The review reports mortality after HFpEF hospitalization ranging from about 15 percent at 1 year to 75 percent at 5 to 10 years.
The review reports that adjusted all-cause mortality is lower in HFpEF than in HFrEF, with a hazard ratio of 0.68 and 95 percent confidence interval 0.64 to 0.71 in the cited MAGGIC analysis.
The review states that approximately 6 to 10 percent of patients with HFpEF are hospitalized for heart failure each year.
The review states that specific conditions such as transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy require recognition because targeted therapies are available.
The source PDF states that the article was updated on June 9, 2026.

The review recommends diagnosing HFpEF by integrating heart failure symptoms and signs, LVEF of at least 50 percent without a prior reduced LVEF, and objective evidence of cardiac structural or functional abnormalities or elevated filling pressures.

The review recommends excluding respiratory disease, ischemic heart disease, hypertensive or valvular heart disease, cardiomyopathies, Fabry disease, and cardiac amyloidosis when evaluating suspected HFpEF.

Figure 1 gives a pragmatic diagnostic pathway that starts with symptoms or signs, ECG and echocardiography, natriuretic peptides, and assessment for HFpEF mimics, then uses structural and hemodynamic evidence when uncertainty remains.
Figure 1 uses left ventricular mass index thresholds of at least 95 g per square meter in women and at least 115 g per square meter in men as evidence of structural abnormality.
Figure 1 uses relative wall thickness greater than 0.42 as a structural threshold.
Figure 1 uses left atrial volume index greater than 34 mL per square meter in sinus rhythm and greater than 40 mL per square meter in atrial fibrillation as structural thresholds.
Figure 1 uses E to e-prime greater than 9 at rest and greater than 15 with exercise as echocardiographic evidence supporting elevated filling pressure.
Figure 1 uses NT-proBNP of at least 125 pg per mL in sinus rhythm and greater than 365 pg per mL in atrial fibrillation as supportive thresholds.

Figure 1 uses pulmonary artery systolic pressure greater than 35 mm Hg and tricuspid regurgitation velocity greater than 2.8 m per second at rest or greater than 3.4 m per second with exercise as supportive thresholds.

Figure 1 uses pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of at least 15 mm Hg at rest, at least 25 mm Hg during exercise, or a pulmonary capillary wedge pressure to cardiac output slope of at least 2 mm Hg per L per minute as invasive evidence of HFpEF.
Figure 1 uses left ventricular end-diastolic pressure of at least 16 mm Hg as an invasive hemodynamic threshold.
The review reports that an NT-proBNP cutoff of 125 pg per mL has sensitivity 0.98, specificity 0.35, and negative predictive value 0.97 for ruling out heart failure in the cited diagnostic study.
The review notes that natriuretic peptide concentrations may be falsely high with renal impairment or atrial fibrillation and inappropriately low in obesity.
The review states that available HFpEF diagnostic scores lack robust validation and that the diagnosis remains in doubt in approximately 30 percent of patients.

When noninvasive testing does not establish HFpEF, the review recommends considering invasive hemodynamic testing at rest or during exercise, diastolic stress testing, or cardiac magnetic resonance imaging when a mimic is suspected.

The review states that current HFpEF treatment goals are symptom relief, improved quality of life, and fewer heart failure hospitalizations because no available medical therapy has shown a significant mortality reduction in HFpEF.

The review notes that many treatment trials enrolled patients with LVEF greater than 40 or 45 percent rather than the contemporary HFpEF threshold of at least 50 percent, which limits direct inference to strict HFpEF.

The review emphasizes treatment of underlying causes and coexisting conditions such as hypertension, obesity, diabetes, atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease, ischemic heart disease, and sleep apnea.

The review reports that CHARM-Preserved did not significantly reduce its primary composite with candesartan, hazard ratio 0.89 and 95 percent confidence interval 0.77 to 1.03, although heart failure hospitalization was 15 percent with candesartan versus 18 percent with placebo, P=0.02.
The review reports that I-PRESERVE did not significantly reduce its primary composite with irbesartan, hazard ratio 0.95 and 95 percent confidence interval 0.86 to 1.05.

The review reports that PEP-CHF did not significantly reduce its primary composite with perindopril, hazard ratio 0.92 and 95 percent confidence interval 0.70 to 1.21, but heart failure hospitalization at 1 year was lower, hazard ratio 0.63 and 95 percent confidence interval 0.41 to 0.97.

The review reports that PARAGON-HF enrolled 4822 patients with LVEF above 45 percent and found a rate ratio of 0.87 with 95 percent confidence interval 0.75 to 1.01 and P=0.06 for total heart failure hospitalizations and cardiovascular death with sacubitril-valsartan.
The review reports a PARAGON-HF subgroup signal in women, rate ratio 0.73 with 95 percent confidence interval 0.59 to 0.90.
The review reports a PARAGON-HF subgroup signal in participants with LVEF below the median of 57 percent, rate ratio 0.78 with 95 percent confidence interval 0.64 to 0.95.
The review reports that PARAGLIDE-HF found a sacubitril-valsartan to valsartan NT-proBNP geometric mean ratio of 0.85 with a printed 95 percent confidence interval of 0.73 to 0.10.

The printed PARAGLIDE-HF confidence interval of 0.73 to 0.10 is internally impossible because the upper bound is below both the lower bound and the point estimate. The extraction preserves the printed values without correction.
The review reports more symptomatic hypotension with sacubitril-valsartan in PARAGLIDE-HF, odds ratio 1.73 with 95 percent confidence interval 1.09 to 2.76.

The review reports that PARALLAX found an NT-proBNP geometric mean ratio of 0.84 with 95 percent confidence interval 0.80 to 0.88 for sacubitril-valsartan versus individualized medical therapy but no improvement in 6-minute walk distance.

The review states that Aldo-DHF randomized 422 patients and that spironolactone 25 mg improved cardiac structure, biomarkers, and diastolic function but did not improve symptoms, signs, or quality of life.
The review states that TOPCAT did not reduce its primary composite outcome with spironolactone in patients with LVEF above 45 percent.

The review states that FINEARTS-HF showed finerenone reduced the composite of cardiovascular death and total heart failure events in patients with LVEF at least 40 percent and supports finerenone as a treatment option.

The review notes beta-blocker use in up to 80 percent of patients with HFpEF but states that randomized data with nebivolol and carvedilol have not shown reductions in death or heart failure hospitalization or consistent quality-of-life benefit.
The review recommends diuretics to treat congestion and symptoms, using the lowest dose needed after euvolemia and considering reduction or discontinuation when congestion resolves.
The review states that loop diuretics are used in approximately 90 percent of patients with acute heart failure and that thiazides may be added for persistent congestion or hypertension.

The review reports that EMPEROR-Preserved found empagliflozin 10 mg daily reduced cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalization, hazard ratio 0.79 with 95 percent confidence interval 0.69 to 0.90 and P<0.001.

The review reports that DELIVER found dapagliflozin 10 mg daily reduced worsening heart failure or cardiovascular death, hazard ratio 0.82 with 95 percent confidence interval 0.73 to 0.92 and P<0.001.
The review reports a pooled hazard ratio of 0.80 with 95 percent confidence interval 0.73 to 0.87 and P<0.001 for cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalization with SGLT2 inhibitors.
The review reports that the pooled SGLT2 inhibitor benefit was driven by fewer heart failure hospitalizations, hazard ratio 0.74 with 95 percent confidence interval 0.67 to 0.83 and P<0.001.
The review reports no statistically significant pooled reduction in cardiovascular death with SGLT2 inhibitors, hazard ratio 0.88 with 95 percent confidence interval 0.77 to 1.00 and P=0.052.

The review states that contemporary guidelines recommend SGLT2 inhibitors for HFpEF based on the composite trial endpoints while emphasizing that the observed benefit is mainly fewer heart failure hospitalizations.
The review reports that STEP-HFpEF with semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly improved KCCQ score by 16.6 points versus 8.7 with placebo, P<0.001.
The review reports that STEP-HFpEF produced mean body-weight change of minus 13.3 percent with semaglutide versus minus 2.6 percent with placebo, P<0.001.
The review reports that STEP-HFpEF improved 6-minute walk distance by 21.5 m with semaglutide versus 1.2 m with placebo, P<0.001.
The review reports that STEP-HFpEF reduced C-reactive protein by 43.5 percent with semaglutide versus 7.3 percent with placebo, P<0.001.

The review states that STEP-HFpEF DM showed similar benefit in patients with obesity-related HFpEF and type 2 diabetes and that a pooled semaglutide analysis reported fewer major adverse cardiovascular events.

The review reports that SUMMIT enrolled 364 patients with LVEF above 50 percent and obesity and found tirzepatide reduced cardiovascular death or worsening heart failure, hazard ratio 0.62 with 95 percent confidence interval 0.41 to 0.95 and P=0.026.
The review reports that SUMMIT improved KCCQ score by a between-group difference of 6.9 points with 95 percent confidence interval 3.3 to 10.6 and P<0.001.
The review concludes that incretin-based therapies have shown benefit in HFpEF with obesity but states that more trials are needed and that benefit in patients without obesity is unknown.
The review reports that CHAMPION randomized 550 patients and found CardioMEMS-guided therapy reduced heart failure hospitalizations irrespective of LVEF.
The review reports that MONITOR-HF enrolled 348 patients, 28 percent with LVEF above 40 percent, and found mean KCCQ change of 7.05 with CardioMEMS monitoring versus minus 0.08 with usual care.
The review states that REDUCE LAP-HF II did not show benefit from an interatrial shunt for its composite primary endpoint.
The review reports that RELIEVE-HF did not significantly improve its primary outcome, win ratio 0.86 with 95 percent confidence interval 0.61 to 1.22 and P=0.20.

The review reports adverse events in 60.2 percent of preserved-EF patients who received an interatrial shunt versus 35.9 percent who did not in RELIEVE-HF, P=0.001, and interprets this as a possible harm signal.
Table 1 shows that all listed international guidelines recommend diuretics for HFpEF, with class I recommendations in the 2022 ACC-AHA and 2021 or 2023 ESC guidance.
Table 1 lists initial and maximum daily loop-diuretic doses of furosemide 20 to 40 mg and 600 mg, bumetanide 0.5 to 1 mg and 10 mg, and torsemide 10 to 20 mg and 200 mg.

Table 1 lists empagliflozin 10 mg daily and dapagliflozin 10 mg daily for HFpEF and shows SGLT2 inhibitor recommendations of class IIa in 2022 ACC-AHA guidance and class I in the 2023 ESC focused update.
Table 1 lists spironolactone 12.5 to 25 mg initially with a maximum daily dose of 100 mg and shows a class IIb ACC-AHA recommendation for MRAs.
Table 1 lists finerenone 10 mg initially with a maximum daily dose of 40 mg but shows no class recommendation in the guideline columns included in the table.

Table 1 lists candesartan 4 mg to 32 mg, irbesartan 75 mg to 300 mg, losartan 25 mg to 150 mg, valsartan 20 mg to 160 mg, and sacubitril-valsartan 24-26 mg twice daily to 97-103 mg twice daily as RAS or ARNI dosing options.

The review explains that guideline differences for SGLT2 inhibitors reflect the timing of trial publications and that the 2023 ESC focused update gives SGLT2 inhibitors a class I recommendation for HFpEF.

The review states that U.S. and Japanese guidance gives class IIb recommendations for ARNIs and MRAs in HFpEF, Canadian guidance suggests RAS inhibitors and MRAs, and ESC guidance does not recommend those agents for HFpEF because the supporting signals came from subgroups of trials with negative primary outcomes.
The review states that HFpEF classification and diagnostic criteria remain uncertain and that the LVEF-based term is nonspecific and rests on an arbitrary cutoff for a heterogeneous disease.
The review states that more disease-modifying therapies are needed and that phenotypic subgroups may require specific treatments.
The review states that whether GLP-1 receptor agonists and GIP agonists benefit patients with HFpEF who are not obese is unknown.
The review calls for more specific noninvasive diagnostic tools, biomarkers, and techniques to estimate intracardiac pressures and volumes.
The review states that no single HFpEF therapy trial has shown a significant reduction in mortality or cardiovascular death despite reductions in composite morbidity and mortality endpoints.
For the case patient, the authors recommend intravenous diuretics for pulmonary and systemic congestion followed by an oral loop diuretic after euvolemia.
For the case patient, the authors recommend adding an SGLT2 inhibitor to reduce symptoms and the risk of subsequent heart failure hospitalization.
For the case patient, the authors recommend treating resistant hypertension and obesity and would add spironolactone if blood pressure remains above 130 over 80 mm Hg despite ramipril and amlodipine.
For the case patient, the authors would consider a GLP-1 receptor agonist for obesity.
For the case patient, the authors recommend assessment for sleep-disordered breathing and treatment of obstructive sleep apnea if present.
The authors recommend healthy lifestyle measures, monitoring disease progression, and treating coexisting conditions to reduce future hospitalizations and improve quality of life.
The article states that disclosure forms provided by the authors are available with the full text at NEJM.org; the disclosure forms were not included in the selected source packet.
